content.title: Understanding Fringe Groups: Why They Form and How to Connect
content.text: A Communication Theory PerspectiveHave you ever noticed how important communication is to building a strong community? As someone who just graduated from the Communication Studies program at West Virginia University , I’m passionate about using communication to bridge divides. In this blog , I want to explore different communication styles — how we talk to each other one-on-one, in groups, online, and compassionately.Think of fringe groups as the outliers in society. They often have strong beliefs that some might consider extreme. Sure, some people join these groups for a sense of belonging, but they can also spread negativity and distrust.So how can we bridge these gaps? Nonviolent communication is a powerful tool for understanding people with different beliefs, even online. By exploring how online spaces influence these groups, we can all learn to communicate better and build a more accepting community.Let’s break down what fringe groups are all about. They’re basically groups with ideas on the fringes of society, sometimes even considered radical. They might have unpopular views and advocate for controversial actions. These groups can be political, religious, or social, and they can pop up in response to current events or bigger trends. Even though they might be on the outskirts, fringe groups can have a big impact on society and even influence laws and public opinion.Press enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Antenna on UnsplashTalking to People With Different Beliefs: Challenges and SolutionsThese days, it can be tough to have conversations with people who have totally different views than you, especially if they belong to a fringe group. The way you act during these talks can make a big difference in how the other person responds. Experts in how people communicate (called interpersonal communication specialists) say that everyone’s behavior in a conversation directly affects the other person’s reaction, either positive or negative [1].For example, at work, being friendly with your colleagues usually leads to them being nice back. But if someone isn’t pulling their weight, that friendliness can backfire [2]. When someone listening makes the other person feel safe and comfortable, the speaker is more likely to open up and share their thoughts and feelings, which can create a stronger bond [2].A study on small group communication [3] showed that in groups where there’s pressure to agree and everyone seems similar, people are more likely to talk to those with the most extreme viewpoints. The study also found that these groups tended to become more uniform in their thinking [3].There are a lot of things that can influence how people interact with each other, especially when dealing with someone who has strong, uncommon beliefs. Two theories, Social Penetration Theory and Muted Group Theory, can be helpful for understanding how to connect with these people.Creating a Safe Space for Open CommunicationSocial Penetration Theory says that relationships develop by gradually revealing personal information to each other [4]. However, for fringe groups, there might be big differences in values and beliefs compared to mainstream society. A study by Baack et al. explored how Social Penetration Theory can help understand ethical issues [5]. They found it can also explain why someone might act unethically and how this theory can be useful for managers and researchers [5]. It basically helps identify potential problems before they get out of hand.The power dynamics within these groups can also make it harder for people to open up. Because of that, creating a safe and respectful space for fringe groups to share their personal information is key. This environment encourages honest and open communication, which can build trust and understanding between these groups and the larger community. Here are some ways to create a safe space for people from fringe groups to share their beliefs:Have Conversations to Understand Their PerspectiveStart discussions aimed at understanding the values, beliefs, and ideas of fringe groups. These conversations can be challenging, but it’s important to approach them with an open mind and really listen to what they have to say. By doing this, we can build trust and understanding between mainstream groups and fringe groups. Remember, empathy and understanding are essential for creating a safe and inclusive space for everyone, regardless of their beliefs.2. Be Aware of Power ImbalancesMuted Group Theory is a concept that highlights the role of language in shaping our experiences and how we interact with the world [6]. It wasn’t originally designed for interpersonal communication, but it can help us be more aware of the challenges faced by marginalized groups when they talk to others. According to this theory, the dominant group in society has more control over how things are described [6]. This means their voices are often heard more clearly, while the voices of marginalized groups might be ignored or dismissed. People from marginalized groups often have trouble expressing their ideas without being judged, silenced, or discriminated against [7]. Additionally, mainstream culture can misrepresent their experiences, leading to misunderstandings [7].By recognizing the power imbalances and societal norms that can prevent certain groups from fully expressing themselves, we can work towards creating communication environments that are more inclusive and supportive [7]. This means actively listening, acknowledging and respecting the experiences of others, and being open to learning about different perspectives.3. Create a Space for Fair CommunicationThe principles of Muted Group Theory and Social Penetration Theory can be applied to create a more balanced and inclusive space for communication between anyone, from friends and family to neighbors and even strangers. By following these theories, we can work towards building communities that are more understanding and empathetic, where both fringe and mainstream groups can be heard and learn from each other. This can help us create a fairer society where everyone feels valued and respected.Understanding Our Groups: How We Connect and Why We Sometimes ClashOur world is full of all kinds of groups — from sports teams to religious communities to political parties. But what happens when groups start forming around extreme beliefs or prejudices? These fringe groups, as they’re called, can be pretty scary. They often have a strong sense of “us vs. them” and can be really hostile to outsiders.Gordon Allport’s classic book “The Nature of Prejudice” (published way back in 1954!) helps us understand how prejudice and group behavior work. Here are some key ideas to keep in mind:Power and Perception: It all boils down to power imbalances and feeling threatened. Think about how privilege and discrimination play out — it can lead to some serious problems (Allport, 1954). To challenge these imbalances, we need to educate ourselves on social justice issues and listen to the experiences of those who are marginalized.Finding Our Tribes: We all crave that sense of belonging, and that’s where ingroups come in. These are the groups we feel connected to, like our family or friend circle (Hogg, 2023). But it’s important to remember that groups aren’t set in stone — we can move between them based on our needs. Understanding this can help us navigate group dynamics and avoid conflicts.Keeping Up With the Joneses: We all compare ourselves to others, and that includes the groups we identify with. These “reference groups” can be based on race, religion, or even nationality (Hogg, 2023; Allport, 1954). For example, we might compare our experiences to those in the majority group. Being aware of these comparisons can help us avoid stereotypes and prejudices.Get Celine M. Wilson’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.Remember me for faster sign inFeeling Lost, Joining a Cause: Sometimes, people who feel uncertain about themselves are drawn to fringe groups that offer a clear identity. The problem is, these groups can be pretty extreme — think racist, xenophobic, or super nationalistic (Hogg, 2023). They often have strict leaders who don’t tolerate different viewpoints, and that just creates a big divide. The key here is to stay open-minded and promote a more inclusive society.When Worlds Collide: Now, imagine people from different backgrounds coming together. It can be awkward! They might start questioning their own beliefs or feeling unsure how to act. This uncertainty can lead to misunderstandings and conflicts. But there’s hope! By fostering empathy and understanding, we can build stronger relationships across groups.The Root of Uncertainty: A lot of prejudice comes from simply not knowing what to think about other groups. Psychologists say this is “uncertainty-identity theory” in action (Hogg, 2007). Basically, when we’re unsure about ourselves, we seek out groups that make us feel secure.Studies have shown that this uncertainty comes in two flavors: uncertainty about ourselves as individuals, and uncertainty about whether we truly belong to a group (Wagoner et al., 2017). Both of these can make us feel less connected to our groups.This is important because it helps us understand why people might feel excluded or threatened. By creating a more welcoming environment, we can help everyone feel like they belong. And that’s how we build a society based on mutual respect and understanding.Online Groups: Finding Your Crew and Avoiding the Dark SideThe internet has become our modern-day town square, with online communities popping up for everything under the sun. These groups are awesome for connecting with people who share your interests, no matter where you live. But with all this connection comes some challenges, especially when it comes to fringe groups with extreme views.The Psychology of “Us vs. Them” OnlineThere’s this cool model called the SIDE Model that helps explain why people might join these online groups. Basically, it boils down to feeling like you belong. Online anonymity can make you feel less like yourself and more like part of a team. The more time you spend in a group, the stronger that feeling of belonging becomes, which can be good for shyness, but it can also make you less critical of the group’s ideas.Why We Over-Share Online (and How it Can Be a Good Thing)Studies show people tend to open up more online, especially if they can’t be seen. It’s kind of like spilling your guts to a stranger in a dark bar — anonymity reduces your self-consciousness and lets you be more honest. This can actually be a good thing, allowing people to explore their thoughts and feelings more freely.Tips for Thriving in Online CommunitiesSo, how do you navigate these online spaces and make sure they’re positive experiences? Here are a few tips:Remember: You’re Not Just a Username. Anonymity can be a double-edged sword. It can make you feel free to be yourself, but it can also lead to people acting rudely or following the crowd blindly. Be mindful of this and try to have respectful conversations even if you disagree.Don’t Get Sucked into the Groupthink. We all have a natural tendency to favor our own “team.” This can be great for group bonding, but it can also lead to prejudice against outsiders. Be open to other perspectives and try to see things from different angles.Make it a Positive Space. If you’re part of an online community, set the tone for respectful discussion. Be kind, avoid personal attacks, and remember there are real people behind the usernames. By fostering a welcoming environment, you can make the online experience enjoyable for everyone.Online communities can be a great way to connect and learn. By understanding how they work and following these tips, you can make sure your online experience is positive and productive.Talking it Out: How NVC Can Help People in Fringe GroupsImagine someone you know gets mixed up with a radical group. Yikes! It’s easy to want to lecture them, but what if there’s a better way? That’s where Nonviolent Communication (NVC) comes in.Think of NVC as a toolbox for understanding people, even those with far-out views. It helps us see what needs aren’t being met that might be pushing them towards these groups. Maybe they crave a sense of belonging, or feel like their voice isn’t heard.Here’s the key: NVC isn’t about judging or calling them wrong. It’s about listening — really listening — to their feelings and what’s important to them. We all have basic needs, like feeling safe and connected. When those needs aren’t met, we can lash out or seek out groups that promise to fill that void.NVC gives us some handy tools for these conversations:Listen Up: Pay close attention to what they’re saying, without interrupting or assuming the worst.Feelings, Not Blaming: Talk about how their situation makes them feel, instead of pointing fingers.Needs Underneath: Help them identify the core needs driving their actions. Is it safety? Connection? Purpose?Be Clear: Once you understand their needs, tell them what you need — maybe it’s a more peaceful way to express themselves.People who learn NVC report better relationships and even avoid conflicts. By understanding the “why” behind someone’s involvement in a radical group, we can help them find healthier ways to meet their needs and contribute to society in a positive way.Remember: NVC is a skill that takes practice. But even small steps can make a big difference.
